title: The comet orchid
teaches: What flowers are for, how they make animals carry pollen, the double fertilisation that makes a seed and fruit, and a moth Darwin predicted forty years early

blocks.text: In January 1862 a box of orchids arrived at Charles Darwin's house from James Bateman, a grower who knew Darwin was writing a book on how orchids are pollinated. Among them was a flower from Madagascar, *Angraecum sesquipedale*, now called the comet orchid or Darwin's orchid: a waxy white star, and hanging below it a green tube, a **spur**, almost 30 centimetres long. Only the bottom few centimetres of the spur held nectar. "Good Heavens what insect can suck it," Darwin wrote to a friend.

In his orchid book that year, Darwin made a prediction. Somewhere in Madagascar there must be a moth with a tongue ten or eleven inches long, 25 to 28 centimetres, long enough to reach that nectar. Some entomologists doubted it. In 1867 Alfred Russel Wallace backed him: a tropical American hawkmoth already known had a tongue almost long enough, and a relative living in Madagascar could reach. In 1903 the moth was described: a big hawkmoth whose tongue, coiled like a watch spring under its head, unrolled to about 25 centimetres. It was named *praedicta*, the predicted one.[^moth] Nobody recorded one actually visiting the orchid in the wild until the 1990s.

Darwin was not guessing blindly. He had a theory of why the spur was so long: the orchid and its moth had lengthened together, each pushing the other. The theory needed the moth. To see how it works, we start with what a flower is for.

Lesson 17's pine throws its pollen to the wind, and most of it is wasted. Flowers do something else: they get animals to carry the pollen from one plant to another of the same kind, which wastes far less. That plants have sexes at all was shown by Rudolf Camerarius in 1694: female mulberry and spinach plants grown away from males set no seed. A century later, in 1793, Christian Konrad Sprengel, a German schoolmaster, published *The Secret of Nature Discovered in the Structure and Fertilisation of Flowers*.[^sprengel]

Sprengel watched insects on flowers for years. He saw that the coloured spots and lines on many petals point toward the nectar, and called them nectar guides. He saw that nectar is hidden where only a visiting insect can reach it, and that reaching it brushes the insect against the pollen and the part that receives pollen. And he saw that many flowers shed their own pollen before they are ready to receive any, so they must get it from another flower. Flowers, he concluded, are built to be visited. His book was largely ignored until Darwin read it.

blocks.caption: The parts of a flower, and the fruit its ovary becomes.

blocks.text: A typical flower has four rings of parts. Outermost are the **sepals**, usually green, which wrapped the bud. Then the **petals**, the advertisement. Then the **stamens**, each a stalk carrying a small pollen sac, the anther. At the centre is the **carpel**, or several fused together: a sticky **stigma** on top to catch pollen, a stalk called the style, and at the base the **ovary**, holding the ovules that will become seeds. Not every flower has all four rings. Grasses, pollinated by wind, have no petals at all.

Each kind of pollinator sees, smells and reaches in its own way, and flowers that rely on one kind tend to share a look. Bee flowers are often blue, purple or yellow with a landing platform. Hummingbird flowers are red and tubular, with no scent, since birds see red well and smell little. Moth flowers are white or pale, open at dusk and smell sweet at night, with nectar at the bottom of a long tube that only a long tongue can reach: the comet orchid is an extreme moth flower. Fly flowers can smell of rotting meat.

blocks.caption: A yellow flower as we see it and as a bee sees it.
blocks.task: See it as a bee does

blocks.text: Bees can't see red, but they see ultraviolet, which we can't. Photographed through an ultraviolet filter, many plain yellow flowers turn out to have a dark centre, a bullseye of Sprengel's nectar guide that only the bee can see. A flower is an advertisement for whoever will carry its pollen, written in that animal's senses.

A pollen grain that lands on a stigma grows a tube down through the style to an ovule, as in the pine of lesson 17, but in flowering plants the tube carries two sperm. In 1898 the Russian botanist Sergei Navashin, studying lilies and fritillaries, found that both are used. One fertilises the egg, which becomes the embryo. The other fuses with a different cell in the ovule, and that becomes a store of food for the embryo, the **endosperm**.[^double] The white of a grain of rice, the flour in wheat and the flesh of a coconut are endosperm. Nearly all other plants fertilise only the egg, and stock the seed beforehand; a flowering plant makes its seed's food store only if the seed has been fertilised, so it spends nothing on seeds that won't grow.

Once its ovules are fertilised, the ovary swells and becomes the **fruit**, with the seeds inside it. A pea pod, a tomato, an apple core, a sunflower seed in its striped shell and a grain of wheat are all fruits in this sense, each an ovary with its seeds.[^apple] Many fruits are built to be eaten by animals that spread the seeds; lesson 19 follows where they go.

Ecology's lesson on the finches of Daphne Major watched selection happen. In a drought, finches with deeper beaks could crack the big tough seeds that were left and survived; their young inherited the deeper beaks, and the average beak changed in a single generation. Nothing in a finch decided to grow a deeper beak. Variation that already existed was sorted by who survived and bred, and because beak depth is partly inherited, the next generation was different. This sorting is **natural selection**.

Darwin's explanation of the spur works the same way. A moth with its tongue in an orchid's spur presses its head against the flower to reach the nectar, and the orchid's pollen sticks to its head. If the spur is shorter than the tongue, the moth can sip without pressing close, and leaves without the pollen. So among the orchids, those whose spurs are longer than the local moths' tongues get more pollen carried and set more seed. Among the moths, those with longer tongues get more nectar, live better and lay more eggs. Each lengthening on one side makes extra length worth having on the other.

blocks.caption: The orchid's spur and the moth's tongue over 300 generations. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then hold the spur fixed and play it

blocks.text: This is **coevolution**: two kinds of living thing changing in step, each a strong source of selection on the other. It explains why the spur is absurdly long. What serves the orchid is not length itself, but being a little longer than its moths' tongues, and once the moths catch up, a little longer again. A spur 30 centimetres long and a tongue to match is what many rounds of that race leave behind. Darwin argued this in 1862, and the moth was what the argument required.

Getting the logic the right way round matters. The flower did not lengthen because it needed to fit the moth, and the moth did not lengthen because it needed to fit the flower. At each step, the ones that happened to be a little longer did a little better, and the next generation was a little longer on average. A rough estimate: if spurs one centimetre longer than average were pollinated 10 percent more often, and length is partly inherited, the average might rise by about a millimetre a generation; the exact figure depends on how much of the variation is inherited. Adding 25 centimetres would then take about 250 generations. An orchid takes several years to flower, so that is a few thousand years. Real rates are unknown, but the time is easily there.

Botanists think most of the flowers in a garden or a meadow were shaped by the same kind of give and take with whatever carries their pollen. Colour, scent, shape, the time of day a flower opens, where it hides its nectar: each is part of an advertisement, tuned over many generations to one kind of visitor and against others that would take the nectar without doing the work. Some flowers cheat their visitors: many orchids offer no nectar at all, and some look and smell enough like a female bee that the males try to mate with them and carry off the pollen.

Take apart a tulip, an apple blossom or a buttercup, and find each ring: sepals, petals, stamens with their dusty anthers, and the carpel in the middle. Cut the ovary across and you'll see the ovules, each of which could have been a seed.

blocks.caption: Six questions on flowers and pollinators
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why did Darwin predict a moth with a tongue about 25 centimetres long?
choices: The comet orchid's nectar sat at the bottom of a 30 cm spur that something must reach to pollinate it
Other orchids with long spurs were pollinated by such moths
Wallace had already seen the moth
items.why: The orchid set seed, so something was pollinating it, and only an animal reaching the bottom of the spur would pick up its pollen. A moth with such a tongue was described in 1903.

items.ask: What part of a flower becomes the fruit?
items.why: After fertilisation the ovary swells into the fruit, and the ovules inside it become the seeds.

items.ask: In a flowering plant, what does the second sperm of each pollen tube do?
choices: Fuses with another cell to make the seed's food store
Fertilises a second egg, making twins
Grows the pollen tube down the style
items.why: One sperm fertilises the egg, making the embryo; the other makes the endosperm, the food store. Navashin found this in 1898.

items.ask: A flower is bright red with a deep tube, and you can't smell it. Which pollinator is it most likely shaped for?
items.why: Birds see red well and smell little; bees can't see red, and moths seek pale, scented flowers at night.

items.ask: Why does an orchid whose spur is longer than the moths' tongues set more seed?
choices: A moth must press its head against the flower to reach the nectar, and picks up the pollen
Moths prefer to visit the longest flowers they can see
items.why: If the spur is shorter than the tongue, the moth sips from a distance and leaves without pollen. A spur longer than the tongue forces contact.

items.ask: Which is the best description of how the spur and tongue got so long?
choices: In each generation, slightly longer ones set more seed or laid more eggs, on both sides in turn
Each species stretched itself to fit the other
Long spurs and tongues appeared together in one big mutation
items.why: Selection sorted variation that already existed. Nothing in either needed or tried to fit the other.

summary: **The comet orchid's nectar sits at the bottom of a 30 cm spur.** Darwin predicted in 1862 a moth to reach it; it was found in 1903.
**Flowers get animals to carry their pollen.** Sprengel (1793) saw that nectar guides, hidden nectar and timing make visitors do the work.
**A typical flower has four rings.** Sepals, petals, stamens making pollen, and the carpel: stigma, style and an ovary holding ovules.
**Flowers are tuned to their pollinators' senses.** Bees see ultraviolet but not red; birds see red; moths find pale, scented flowers at night.
**Flowering plants fertilise twice.** One sperm makes the embryo, the other the seed's food store (Navashin, 1898).
**The ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules the seeds.** A pea pod, a tomato and a grain of wheat are all fruits.
**Spur and tongue lengthened together by selection.** Each step on one side made extra length pay on the other: coevolution, with no need or intention.

double.title: Three sets
double.text: The second sperm fuses with a cell that already has two sets of chromosomes, so most endosperm has three sets, two from the mother and one from the father. In some seeds, such as beans and peas, the embryo absorbs the endosperm as the seed ripens and stores the food in its own first leaves instead.

moth.title: The predicted moth
moth.text: Walter Rothschild and Karl Jordan described Madagascar's long-tongued hawkmoth in 1903 as a subspecies of an African moth and named it *praedicta*. In 2021 it was raised to a species of its own, *Xanthopan praedicta*.

sprengel.title: The rector of Spandau
sprengel.text: Sprengel was headmaster of the town school in Spandau, near Berlin. He began watching wildflowers in 1787 and became so absorbed in them that he neglected his sermons and his school, and was dismissed from his post in 1794, the year after his book came out. He spent the rest of his life giving private lessons and leading botanical walks around Berlin.

apple.title: What the rest of an apple is
apple.text: In an apple or a pear, only the tough core around the pips comes from the ovary. The crisp flesh we eat grows from the base of the flower, which wraps around the ovary and swells after fertilisation.
